checks.demonstration: Read the combinatorial decomposition, score construction, projection matrices and hardmax limit. An equality class of the combined query/key tuple is specified by each tuple internal type plus all cross equalities. Orthonormal IDs turn dot products into equality indicators. Assign positive signs to required equalities and negative signs to required inequalities; type-ID dot products add strict penalties for wrong types. Every compatible key attains the same maximal score, while each incompatible one has a positive gap. Scaling by a makes total incompatible softmax mass decay exponentially; compatible keys receive uniform mass, exactly the normalized basis row in the limit. For rows with no compatible key normalization is undefined; the source explicitly flags this and masks their contributions to zero in the later FFN construction.
checks.scope: Does not certify the entire subsequent multilayer universality result or uniform approximation over unbounded feature inputs. The k=1 singleton-type case needs no type penalty; node equality/inequality alone supplies the gap. Practical truncated/random positional features do not satisfy exact orthonormality automatically.
checks.claimContext: Attention can approximate the normalized nonzero rows of the equality-pattern basis tensors using distinguishing node identifiers and the stated score construction.

checks.claim: Cross-reconstruction forces every branch to discard uncorrelated modality-specific noise.
checks.explanation: Reconstructing both targets does not require a minimal representation of their shared information. An action token can retain an action-specific nuisance that its visual decoder ignores. Because the same token must also reconstruct its own modality, removing that nuisance can increase the objective.
checks.demonstration:
Let $C$ and $N$ be independent fair bits. Take visual target $(1,C)$, action target $(C,N)$, and constant conditioning state and current frame. The action and fused tokens can encode $(C,N)$; the visual token can encode only $C$. A shared codebook with six entries accommodates all four action/fused codes and the two visual codes.

Let the shared visual decoder return $(1,C)$ from every code. Let the action decoder return $(C,N)$ for the action/fused codes and $(C,1/2)$ for the visual codes. Visual loss is zero, and commitment loss can be zero by placing encoder outputs on the codewords. The summed action MSE is

$$0+0+\mathbb E(N-1/2)^2=\frac14.$$

If every branch discards $N$, each action reconstruction instead incurs variance $1/4$, giving total $3/4$. The visual branch cannot do better than $1/4$ because it never observes the independent bit. Thus retaining private noise achieves the smaller, globally optimal reconstruction loss in this example.

This distinction matters: preserving a general functional relation is weaker than preserving an additive-noise family.
checks.demonstration:
Consider any affine Gaussian acyclic structural model with independent node noises of positive variance, and $m$ iid cells. Write its equations as
$$X_j=b_j+\sum_{k\in\operatorname{pa}(j)}a_{jk}X_k+\varepsilon_j.$$
Let the common aggregation be the smooth nonlinear map
$$g(u_1,\ldots,u_m)=\sinh\!\left(\frac1m\sum_i u_i\right).$$
For $Z_j=g((X_{j,i})_i)$ and $E_j=g((\varepsilon_{j,i})_i)$, the exact aggregate relation is
$$Z_j=\sinh\!\left(b_j+\sum_k a_{jk}\operatorname{arsinh}(Z_k)+\operatorname{arsinh}(E_j)\right).$$
This supplies the general $h$ required by Definition 4.1. The transformed aggregate noises remain independent across nodes and independent of the relevant parent variables.

All conditional-independence patterns also agree with the micro Gaussian model. If its covariance is $\Sigma$, the vector of cell means has covariance $\Sigma/m$; common positive scaling preserves every Gaussian conditional-covariance zero. Applying the coordinatewise bijection $\sinh$ preserves the corresponding sigma-algebras and hence every conditional independence. Thus a nonlinear $g$ preserves both defined properties throughout this affine Gaussian subclass.

$$A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1&0\\1&2&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}.$$
This matrix is positive definite and is realized by one supplied task map $\widetilde H=A^{1/2}$. The true map can remain $H=I$, a noisy rotation; misspecifying the supplied map is allowed by the general formulation. With positive Gaussian source and target noise, neighborhoods of these responses and source estimates have positive probability.

Every interpolant has first coordinate one. Minimizing its penalty gives
$$\min_{\beta_2,\beta_3}\left(2+2\beta_2+2\beta_2^2+\beta_3^2\right),$$
whose unique solution is $\beta_0=(1,-1/2,0)^\top$. The printed expression instead gives $X^+y=(1,0,0)^\top$, because $r=0$. For any full-row-rank $X$, put $a=A^{-1}r$. The limit minimizes $(\beta-a)^\top A(\beta-a)$ subject to $X\beta=y$. Lagrange multipliers give
$$\beta_0=a+A^{-1}X^\top(XA^{-1}X^\top)^{-1}(y-Xa).$$

checks.claim: Averaged m-nearest-neighbor distance recovers the complete density order with probability tending to one.
checks.explanation: The proof uses an interior nearest-neighbor volume formula uniformly up to the boundary. At a boundary, neighbors occupy only one side of a small interval. That geometric difference can make a higher-density point have a larger neighbor distance than a lower-density interior point. The assumptions do not exclude this.
checks.demonstration:
Use the admissible one-dimensional density
\[
p(z)=\frac23(1+z),\qquad z\in[0,1],
\]
and \(m=\lfloor K^{3/4}\rfloor\). This density integrates to one and lies between \(2/3\) and \(4/3\). Let \(Z_{\max}\) be the largest sample, and let \(Z_{\rm mid}\) be the sample at empirical probability \(5/12\), so \(Z_{\rm mid}\to1/2\). Then \(p(Z_{\max})>p(Z_{\rm mid})\) with probability tending to one.

The empirical-CDF error is \(O_{\mathbb P}(\sqrt{\log K/K})=o(m/K)\). Local inversion of the smooth CDF therefore gives the usual order-spacing averages. At \(Z_{\max}\) they are one-sided; near \(1/2\) they are two-sided:
\[
\frac K m\bar R_m(Z_{\max})\ \longrightarrow
\frac1{2p(1)}=\frac38,\qquad
\frac K m\bar R_m(Z_{\rm mid})\ \longrightarrow
\frac1{4p(1/2)}=\frac14.
\]
The higher-density sample thus has the larger averaged distance with probability tending to one. Including the query itself among its neighbors changes only lower-order terms. The asserted complete-order probability tends to zero on this example.
checks.repair:
Replace complete ordering under the current assumptions with a qualified ranking result. Boundary geometry needs correction or an interior-domain restriction, and complete ordering also needs a density-separation condition. A sufficient precise statement is: if a density estimate satisfies
\[
\max_j|\widehat p(Z_j)-p(Z_j)|\le e_K,
\]
then every pair with true density gap greater than \(2e_K\) is ordered correctly by \(\widehat p\). This follows by subtracting the two error bounds. Exact total ordering additionally requires every nonzero sample density gap to exceed \(2e_K\); it does not follow from consistency alone.

checks.explanation: The selected ratio does not cap a jump's benefit at the remaining quota. It can buy expensive coverage that is irrelevant to feasibility. Backwards pruning lowers selected levels but cannot replace them with a cheaper, previously unselected rank.
checks.demonstration:
Take \(n_1=4\), \(K=2\), \(d=1\), and \(\tau=1\), corresponding to \(\alpha=3/4\). Use distance columns
\[
E_{\cdot,1}=(1,100,100,100)^\top,\qquad
E_{\cdot,2}=(2,2.01,2.02,2.03)^\top.
\]
The first column's best gain-to-cost ratio is \(1\). The second column's full jump has ratio \(4/2.03>1\), so the printed rule selects it. Pruning lowers that rank to its first level, costing \(2\) and covering the required point. The optimum selects the first column's first level and costs \(1\). The claimed factor is \(1+\log1=1\), so it is violated even after pruning.

These are legal nonnegative distance-matrix inputs to the stated proxy algorithm. They are also realizable on the line with response zero and the two generated centers at the displayed distances for each row. With two centers their nearest-neighbor ranking scores tie, so a fixed index tie rule supplies the column order.
checks.repair:
Cap each jump's marginal coverage gain \(g_{\rm raw}\) at the remaining quota \(R=\tau-|U|\): use \(g=\min(g_{\rm raw},R)\) in its ratio. This modification has the claimed harmonic guarantee.

At any current level vector, extend each rank toward an optimal level vector. The total extension cost is at most \(\mathrm{OPT}\), by separability and monotonicity of rank costs, and the capped gains sum to at least \(R\). Some available jump therefore has gain-to-cost ratio at least \(R/\mathrm{OPT}\). The chosen jump costs at most \(\mathrm{OPT}\,g/R\). Charging this cost across the \(g\) units of remaining coverage and summing gives
\[
\mathrm{Cost}\le H_\tau\,\mathrm{OPT}
\le(1+\log\tau)\,\mathrm{OPT}.
\]
Positive-gain zero-cost jumps can be taken first. Feasibility-preserving pruning can only reduce the final cost.
checks.scope: This concerns the finite Stage 2 proxy guarantee, including its pruning step. The sufficient repair changes the greedy ratio and proves that proxy bound. It neither challenges nor certifies the separate conformal calibration theorem.

checks.location: Lemma 1 / Appendix B.1 final maximization; Theorem 1 / Appendix A Eqs. (7)-(8)
checks.claim: \mathcal{L}_{S}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\geqslant\ln\left[K-4(K-1)\epsilon\right]
checks.explanation: Appendix B proves a scalar concentration bound for each fixed unitary, then applies it to the maximum over all unitaries without a uniform-concentration argument. This changes the quantifier. The resulting trace-distance bound is false: an average of $M$ pure states has rank at most $M$, so its trace distance from $I_d/d$ is at least $1-M/d$. This also leaves enough capacity for a learned circuit to memorize a training set even when both class distributions have the same population density matrix.
checks.demonstration:
The concentration step must hold uniformly over the circuit chosen from the training data. Two constructions show why a scalar bound for each fixed unitary does not provide that conclusion.

For Lemma 1, draw a feature vector with independent Rademacher coordinates and amplitude-encode it as $|\psi\rangle=d^{-1/2}(\pm1,\ldots,\pm1)$. Its density matrix $\rho=|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|$ has mean $I_d/d$: diagonal entries are $1/d$, and off-diagonal entries have mean zero. For any $M$ samples, the empirical mean $\bar\rho=M^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^M\rho_i$ has rank at most $M$. Let $P$ project onto its kernel. Then
$$\operatorname{Tr}(P\bar\rho)=0,\qquad \operatorname{Tr}(P I_d/d)\ge1-M/d.$$
The variational characterization of trace distance therefore gives
$$D_{\rm tr}(\bar\rho,I_d/d)\ge1-M/d.$$
With $d=256$, $M=32$ and $\epsilon=1/2$, the distance is at least $7/8$ for every sample. Lemma 1 nevertheless assigns probability at least $1-4e^{-4}\approx0.9267$ to distance at most $1/2$. These events cannot both have the stated probabilities.

For Theorem 1, take two classes that each independently sample uniform computational-basis vectors in dimension $d=2^{36}$. Their population density matrices are identical, both $I_d/d$. Draw $m=8192$ samples per class and set $\epsilon=1/8$. A union bound over the $m^2$ cross-class pairs shows that, with probability at least
$$1-\frac{m^2}{d}=\frac{1023}{1024},$$
no basis vector occurs in both classes. Within-class repeats cause no difficulty.

Fix the two observables to be Pauli $Z$ on the first and second qubits. Their joint $(+1,-1)$ and $(-1,+1)$ eigenspaces each have dimension $d/4>m$. On the no-collision event, map each distinct observed vector of class one into a distinct basis vector of the first eigenspace, and each distinct observed vector of class two into the second. These assignments form an injective partial basis permutation and extend to a full permutation. Choose that permutation from a fixed universal circuit family. The family is fixed before sampling, but the optimized member may depend on the data, as allowed by the theorem; no depth, parameter-count or efficiency restriction excludes it.

Every training example then has correct-class logit $+1$ and other-class logit $-1$, yielding training cross-entropy
$$\log(1+e^{-2})\approx0.12693<\log(3/2)\approx0.40547,$$
below the claimed barrier. This happens with probability at least $1023/1024\approx0.99902$, whereas the theorem permits failure probability only $8e^{-16}\approx9.0\times10^{-7}$. The obstruction is the change from concentration for a unitary fixed independently of the data to a bound on the maximum over all unitaries. Identical population density matrices do not prevent an unrestricted learned circuit from fitting the finite training sample.
checks.repair: Replace Lemma 1 by a trace-distance concentration statement with the required dimension dependence, or restrict the circuit and readout class and prove a uniform bound using its complexity. A circuit fixed independently of the data permits scalar concentration with the appropriate union bounds, but that is a narrower quantifier than a circuit optimized on the sample. A separate population statement is available: for balanced classes with identical class-conditional mean density matrices, population cross-entropy is at least $\log K$, where $K$ is the number of classes. These narrower results do not establish the stated unrestricted training-loss barrier.
checks.scope: The contradiction concerns Theorem 1 and Lemma 1 of arXiv v1 under their unrestricted circuit and optimizer quantifiers. It does not assert that the experimental shallow circuits can memorize the construction, or that a trained classifier generalizes.
checks.title: Dimension-free state concentration does not imply a training-loss barrier
checks.claimContext: Theorem 1 asserts an empirical cross-entropy lower bound for every circuit and optimization algorithm when class-conditional population density matrices are close. Its proof uses Lemma 1 to control empirical density matrices in trace distance independently of the number of qubits.
checks.whyItMatters: The central empirical loss barrier fails under its stated quantifiers. Identical population distributions still prevent useful generalization; the example only separates that fact from the ability to fit the training set.

checks.demonstration: Take two replicas and one client \(A\ne c_0\). checks.claim: so the advantage of SWR grows at least linearly in the rollout horizon $T$
checks.explanation: An upper bound on AR error does not force AR to incur that error. Subtracting two upper envelopes supplies no lower bound on the difference between actual errors. The claim fails even with a tight positive per-step error and uniformly bounded finite-codebook refresh distortion.
checks.demonstration:
Use scalar frame domain \([0,1]\), true frames constantly zero, and a predictor that always outputs one, independent of its context. Set
\[
\epsilon=1,\qquad\alpha=0,\qquad\delta_q=1,\qquad W=1,\qquad T=4.
\]
A1 holds for every context and is tight on the correct context. Let the finite-codebook decode/re-encode map be constantly one; its distortion is at most one everywhere in the frame domain, so A2 holds uniformly. Every generated frame is one under both methods, and hence
\[
\mathcal E_{\rm AR}(4)=\mathcal E_{\rm SWR}(4)=1.
\]
But the asserted difference lower bound is
\[
4-\left(1+\frac{1+1}{1-0}\right)=1>0.
\]
Thus the claimed zero difference must be at least one. The admissible \(\alpha=0\) satisfies \(\alpha^W<1\); the example needs neither vanishing prediction error nor an overly loose \(\epsilon\).
checks.repair: Compare the proved upper envelopes as envelopes, without asserting an ordering of actual errors. Alternatively add a genuine AR lower bound, such as \(\mathcal E_{\rm AR}(T)\ge cT-d\), justified by a specified noncontractive error mechanism. Together with a separately established SWR upper bound this gives \(\mathcal E_{\rm AR}-\mathcal E_{\rm SWR}\ge cT-d-C_W\). Merely assuming an upper error budget is insufficient. Even under the displayed approximation \(C_W\approx2W\epsilon+\delta_q\), the envelope crossover solves \(T\approx2W+\delta_q/\epsilon\), not \(W+\delta_q/\epsilon\). Neither that arithmetic correction nor the stylized interpretation supplies the missing AR lower bound.
checks.scope: Corollary 2’s lower bound does not follow from A1–A2. The witness leaves the separate SWR upper bound intact; an actual-error advantage needs a genuine AR lower bound.
checks.title: Two error upper bounds do not imply a growing lower bound on advantage
checks.whyItMatters: The assumptions permit both methods to have identical errors at every horizon.
checks.claimContext: Appendix C defines frame errors and their rollout maxima. A1 bounds a next-step error by \(\epsilon+\alpha\eta\), with \(\alpha\in[0,1)\), and A2 bounds decode/re-encode distortion by \(\delta_q\). Equations (11) and (13) give \(\mathcal E_{\rm AR}(T)\le T\epsilon\) and \(\mathcal E_{\rm SWR}(T)\le C_W\). Corollary 2 subtracts them to claim a lower bound on the actual error difference.

checks.claim: \hat{z}_{i}=\mathrm{round}(\tilde{z}_{i})+\bigl(\tilde{z}_{i}-\mathrm{sg}[\mathrm{round}(\tilde{z}_{i})]\bigr),
checks.explanation: In the forward pass the rounded terms cancel exactly, so the displayed output is \(\widetilde z_i\), rather than an integer grid point. The subsequent mixed-radix index therefore need not be integral. This is a failure of the explicitly defined mathematical map, independent of whether an implementation uses that expression.
checks.demonstration:
Since \(\operatorname{sg}(a)=a\) in forward evaluation,
\[
\widehat z_i=\operatorname{round}(\widetilde z_i)+\widetilde z_i-\operatorname{round}(\widetilde z_i)=\widetilde z_i.
\]
For any fixed finite shifts and offsets, the tanh-bounded coordinate has a nonempty open interval as its range, which contains noninteger values. For example, the first, symmetric odd-level coordinate with \(L_1=7\) and zero shift/offset attains \(\widetilde z_1=1/4\) at input \(\operatorname{arctanh}(1/14)\). The printed map returns \(1/4\), whereas rounding returns zero. Place this value in the first mixed-radix coordinate, whose stride is the empty product \(\prod_{j<1}L_j=1\). With all other coordinates integral, the index equals an integer plus \(1/4\), breaking the stated integer-index invariant. Specifying unit stride matters: a larger integer stride could otherwise cancel a fractional denominator. Integer \(\widetilde z_i\) is a positive case where the two forward maps agree. Away from rounding boundaries, the printed surrogate derivative is one; its forward value is the problem.
checks.repair:
Use the standard straight-through expression
\[
\widehat z_i=\widetilde z_i+\operatorname{sg}\!\left[\operatorname{round}(\widetilde z_i)-\widetilde z_i\right].
\]
It has forward value \(\operatorname{round}(\widetilde z_i)\) and surrogate derivative one. Equivalently use \(\operatorname{round}(\widetilde z_i)+\widetilde z_i-\operatorname{sg}[\widetilde z_i]\). This repairs the rounding map’s discrete-forward invariant; the separate bounding endpoints and mixed-radix range should still be checked under their own definitions.
checks.scope: The finding concerns the explicit forward quantizer and finite-grid invariant in Appendix B.2. The corrected straight-through map returns a rounded value with surrogate derivative one.
checks.title: The printed straight-through expression does not quantize its forward value

review-neurips-2026-151561.title: Capacity-Constrained Online Convex Optimization with Delayed Feedback

checks.location: Theorem 3.1, Eq.(1), and Appendix C assertion that squared-norm regularizers are strongly convex
checks.claim: DW-FTRL has this regret bound for an arbitrary norm under Assumptions 2.1-2.2.
checks.explanation: A squared norm is not automatically strongly convex relative to that norm. The proof uses this property for the regularization increments. For the infinity norm it fails, and a legal selection from the update's argmin set can incur linear regret even without delays or varying weights.
checks.demonstration:
Take \(\mathcal K=[-1,1]^2\) with \(\|\cdot\|_\infty\), \(T=10000\), \(\eta_t=0.01\), \(w_t=1\), zero delays, and \(x_1=(0,0)\). Then \(D=2\), the dual norm is \(\|\cdot\|_1\), and \(G=1\). Use 100 linear losses with gradient \((1,0)\), followed by 4950 pairs with gradients \((0,-1),(0,1)\). After cumulative gradient \((a,b)\), an exact minimizer has radius \(r=\min\{0.01(|a|+|b|),1\}\), first coordinate \(-r\), and second coordinate \(-r\) when \(b\geq0\), \(+r\) when \(b<0\). In particular, the legal tie choice at \(b=0\) is negative. For fixed radius, this minimizes the linear term; minimizing \(-(|a|+|b|)r+r^2/(2\eta)\) proves exact optimality. Only the first regularization increment is nonzero, so this is precisely equation (1). The first 100 predictions incur total loss \(-49.5\); every subsequent loss is one. A comparator with first coordinate \(-1\) has total loss \(-100\). Thus
\[R_T=9950.5>\frac{2^2}{2(0.01)}+0.01(10000)=300.\]
The nonuniqueness is substantive: \(\tfrac12\|x\|_\infty^2\) equals \(1/2\) at \((1,1)\), \((1,-1)\), and their midpoint, contradicting any positive strong-convexity modulus along that segment.
checks.repair:
Restrict this squared-norm update to an inner-product norm, or explicitly assume that \(x\mapsto\tfrac12\|x\|^2\) is 1-strongly convex in the chosen geometry. For an inner-product norm, the exact identity
\[\tfrac12\|a-((1-\theta)x+\theta y)\|^2=(1-\theta)\tfrac12\|a-x\|^2+\theta\tfrac12\|a-y\|^2-\tfrac{\theta(1-\theta)}2\|x-y\|^2\]
proves the required property for every center \(a\). Since \(\alpha_s\geq0\) and \(\sum_{s\leq t}\alpha_s=1/\eta_t\), the accumulated regularizer then has modulus \(1/\eta_t\), restoring the stability premise used in the proof. For general norms, replace the squared norm by an explicitly strongly convex regularizer and rederive the bound using its regularization range and modulus.
checks.scope: The arbitrary-norm first-order guarantee is false for the stated argmin update. The corrected witness uses the negative tie at zero cumulative second-coordinate gradient; the opposite tie does not produce the reported large regret. Euclidean first-order guarantees and the already Euclidean bandit specialization are not refuted.
checks.title: The first-order regret bound needs a strongly convex regularizer
checks.whyItMatters: The regularizer controls prediction stability. Without strong convexity in the stated geometry, its flat directions allow the regret to grow linearly.
checks.claimContext: DW-FTRL uses translated squared norms as regularizers. The first-order model permits an arbitrary norm, assumes domain diameter at most \(D\), and bounds each gradient by \(G\) in the dual norm. Theorem 3.1 gives the following weighted regret bound, where \(\mathcal B_t\) is the feedback backlog, \(w_t\) are the weights, and \(\eta_t\) is a nonincreasing learning-rate sequence. Only the separate bandit setting is explicitly restricted to Euclidean geometry.
checks.verificationNote: The source restricts the norm to Euclidean only for bandit feedback. Applying that restriction to the first-order theorem is a repair, not an existing hypothesis.
checks.checkedLocation: Assumptions 2.1–2.2; Section 3.1, equation (1) and Theorem 3.1; Appendix C regularizer-stability argument.

checks.location: Theorem 11, first bullet; proof in Appendix C.4
checks.claim: Uniform structural-regularity testing with sample rate independent of density scale c.
checks.explanation: No issue was found in the checked claims. The source does not require that universal-scale interpretation. Theorem 11 does not label its \(C\) universal, and the following paragraph refers to suitable regularity parameters \(c,r\) for \(P\). Uniform error over the null and alternative within the stated class does not by itself require uniformity over all choices of class parameters. The Gaussian example changes those parameters as its variance grows, so it does not establish the alleged contradiction.
checks.demonstration:
The proposed family is \(P_0=\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2)\), \(P_1=\mathcal N(1,\sigma^2)\), with no truncation. It satisfies the density condition with
\[c_\sigma=\frac{e^{-1/2}}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}},\qquad r_\sigma=\sigma.\]
The calculation \(\mathrm{KL}(P_0^{\otimes n}\|P_1^{\otimes n})=n/(2\sigma^2)\) is correct. Choosing \(\sigma=10\sqrt n\) gives a total-variation upper bound \(1/20\), hence equal-prior testing error at least \(19/40\). This rules out a sample-size constant shared across that changing family of regularity classes.

It does not give the same conclusion in a fixed density-lower-bound class. If that class requires \(f_v(0)\geq c_0>0\), a Gaussian must satisfy
\[\frac1{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\geq c_0,\qquad \sigma\leq\frac1{c_0\sqrt{2\pi}}.\]
Thus the arbitrary-scale sequence cannot remain in that class.

The proof context also retains the scale explicitly. Theorem 9 bounds estimation error by
\[\frac2c\left(\varepsilon+A\sqrt{\frac{d+\log(1/\delta)}n}\right),\]
with a separate local-radius sample condition. Appendix C.4 applies this result to the threshold test \(\mathbf1\{\|\hat\mu\|>\alpha/2\}\). At zero truncation, reducing this error below \(\alpha/2\) entails a sample factor proportional to \(c^{-2}\). A constant depending on the fixed regularity class therefore accommodates exactly the scale dependence exhibited by the Gaussian calculation. The existing example does not refute the source claim.
checks.scope: The proposed Gaussian-scale counterexample changes the theorem’s regularity class and does not refute the stated guarantee.

The earlier objection reads \(C\) as one universal constant across arbitrarily changing density scales.

review-neurips-2026-152111.title: STARE: Surprisal-Guided Token-Level Advantage Reweighting for Policy Entropy Stability

checks.claim: A neural-parameter GRPO ascent step is equivalent to Euclidean logit ascent, giving dH/deta=-A Phi.
checks.explanation: A neural policy updates shared model parameters, not independent logits. With $J=\partial z/\partial\theta$ and $u=e_a-p$, the parameter gradient induces logit velocity $\widehat A JJ^\top u$. Omitting $JJ^\top$ can reverse the entropy derivative, rather than only rescale it.
checks.demonstration:
Take a three-token policy with one scalar parameter and logits
$$z(\theta)=\bigl(\log(3/5)+\theta,\ \log(3/10)+\theta,\ \log(1/10)\bigr).$$
At $\theta=0$, its probabilities are $p=(3/5,3/10,1/10)$. Sample token two with fixed advantage $\widehat A=1$ and evaluate the update on-policy, so the importance ratio is one and clipping is inactive. All probabilities are positive and the logits are smooth.

The Jacobian is $J=(1,1,0)^\top$. Thus the actual parameter-gradient direction is
$$\dot\theta=J^\top(e_2-p)=\frac1{10}.$$
Let $h_v=p_v(-\log p_v-H)$ be the entropy gradient with respect to logits. Since $\sum_vh_v=0$ and $h_3>0$, the chain rule gives
$$\dot H=(J^\top h)\dot\theta=\frac1{10}(h_1+h_2)=-\frac1{10}h_3\approx-0.0140464.$$
In contrast, the independent-logit formula gives
$$h^\top(e_2-p)\approx+0.189583.$$
The two expressions have opposite signs. A centered finite difference along the actual parameter update is also approximately $-0.0140464$.

A complete centered response group can realize this direction. Place the displayed context after a branch in one response, assign the other response the opposite advantage, and make every other context's logits independent of this parameter. Other positions then contribute no parameter gradient. Group normalization and averaging introduce only a positive scale, preserving the sign reversal.
checks.repair:
Use the parameter-space chain rule. For one local unclipped on-policy update,
$$\nabla_\theta\log p_a=J^\top(e_a-p),\qquad \nabla_\theta H=J^\top h,$$
so
$$\dot H=\widehat A\,h^\top JJ^\top(e_a-p).$$
This is the inner product of the entropy and policy parameter gradients and can be computed without forming the full Jacobian. The printed formula remains valid when logits are independent parameters, or when $JJ^\top$ acts as one common positive scalar on the relevant directions and that scalar is absorbed into the step size.

Shared parameters also couple positions. For objective $\sum_t w_t\widehat A_t\log p_{t,a_t}$ and entropy $\sum_s v_sH_s$, with fixed nonnegative weights, the exact derivative is
$$\sum_{s,t}v_sw_t\widehat A_t\,h_s^\top J_sJ_t^\top(e_{a_t}-p_t).$$
Thus a general neural-policy sign depends on the Jacobian geometry and cross-position terms. Restrict the advantage–surprisal sign rule to the independent-logit setting; the corrected derivative supplies the local parameter-gradient calculation without asserting a universal shared-parameter sign rule.
checks.scope: The entropy identity is valid for direct Euclidean logit updates, but not arbitrary neural-parameter GRPO updates. The corrected chain-rule expression covers the actual local gradient. This does not invalidate the reported empirical gains of STARE.
checks.title: Parameter updates change entropy through the logit Jacobian

checks.location: Section 4, Theorem 1; Appendix D.1, Steps 1-2, eqs. (137)-(139)
checks.claim: Rule 1 (gate S = {i : lfdr_spatial(alpha-hat(loc_i),k_i,m_i) <= tau}, then the Sun-Cai running-average rule on the marginal lfdr inside S) controls FDR at tau exactly, for every gate threshold tau and every spatial estimator alpha-hat. The text adds that alpha-hat 'may be arbitrarily mis-specified without affecting validity, only the power changes', and the proof asserts that the gated rejection set R1 is contained in the unrestricted running-average rejection set R.
checks.explanation: The gate changes which null probabilities are being averaged. The location-free scores need not be calibrated after this selection. Re-running the prefix rule inside a subset also need not produce a subset of the unrestricted rejection set; even genuine set containment alone does not make false-discovery proportions monotone.
checks.demonstration:
First, scores \((0.05,0.9,0.95)\), gate \(S=\{1,3\}\), and \(\tau=0.5\) yield restricted rejections \(\{1,3\}\) but unrestricted rejections \(\{1,2\}\), disproving the asserted containment. For an FDR violation, take two hypotheses, one true null with \(m=1\) and \(k\) uniform on \(\{0,1\}\), and one alternative. Set \(a=0.3\), \(b=3\), marginal null fraction \(\bar\alpha=1/2\), and \(\tau=0.4\). The null count probabilities are \((1/2,1/2)\); the alternative Beta–Binomial probabilities are \((10/11,1/11)\). Choose the spatial estimator to output \(0.3\) at the null location and \(1\) at the alternative location. The alternative is always gated out. The null enters only when \(k=0\), since its spatial local FDR values are approximately \(0.190751\) and \(0.702128\). At \(k=0\), its marginal local FDR is \(11/31\approx0.354839<0.4\), so the singleton gate rejects it. At \(k=1\), nothing is rejected. Thus
\[\operatorname{FDR}=\tfrac12\cdot1+\tfrac12\cdot0=0.5>0.4.\]
The null law is exactly Assumption 4; the deterministic misspecified spatial estimator is allowed by the theorem’s quantifier.
checks.repair: Drop exact control for arbitrary spatial estimators. A sufficient Bayesian replacement uses scores \(q_i=\Pr(H_{0,i}\mid\mathcal D)\) calibrated to all information \(\mathcal D\) used by the gate and rejection rule. Any \(\mathcal D\)-measurable rejection set satisfying \(\sum_{i\in\mathcal R}q_i/(|\mathcal R|\vee1)\leq\tau\) then has conditional expected FDP at most \(\tau\), and taking expectations gives FDR control. Establishing this condition for estimated scores requires a separate calibration argument. Merely fitting a gate independently, or replacing the false containment step, does not establish the stated guarantee for the existing marginal scores.
checks.scope: The exact arbitrary-misspecification guarantee in Theorem 1 is false. This example does not show failure for the correctly specified estimator or refute the separately proved flip-invariant folded rule.
checks.whyItMatters: A low average of marginal scores inside the selected gate is not an exact false-discovery guarantee unless those scores remain calibrated after selection.
checks.title: An arbitrary spatial gate can destroy Rule 1’s exact FDR control
checks.claimContext: Rule 1 gates hypotheses by the fitted spatial local FDR and applies a running-average threshold to location-free marginal local FDR scores within the selected set \(S\). Theorem 1 assumes the discrete-uniform null law \(k_i\mid H_{0,i},m_i\sim\operatorname{Unif}\{0,\ldots,m_i\}\), and claims exact FDR control for every spatial estimator, including arbitrary misspecification. Appendix D.1 invokes containment in the unrestricted rejection set at Equation (139).

checks.explanation: A finite count grid has a positive minimum nonzero increment at each fixed budget. This does not supply a budget-independent lower bound. At interior counts proportional to the budget, the likelihood-ratio increment and the score spacing both decrease at order one over the budget.
checks.demonstration:
For \(k=pm+O(1)\), \(p\in(0,1)\), the printed likelihood-ratio increment gives
\[\begin{aligned}\Delta_k\log\operatorname{LR}&=\log\frac{k+a}{k+1}+\log\frac{m-k}{m-k-1+b}\\&=-\frac1m\left(\frac{1-a}{p}+\frac{b-1}{1-p}\right)+O(m^{-2}).\end{aligned}\]

For \(a=0.3,b=3\) this is about \(5.06642\). When \(g(k)\) stays in a compact subset of \((0,1)\), Lemma 7’s own score conversion therefore gives \(|g(k+1)-g(k)|=\Theta(1/m)\).

A sufficient scaling for a vanishing relative drift is \(m\max\{1/N,1/\lambda\}\to0\), alongside uniform constants and an interior threshold. checks.demonstration: Consider a one-step task with a fresh hidden goal \(Z\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/2)\). The observation before the sole action is constant, and \(A\in\{0,1\}\). An exact privileged verifier gives terminal reward \(+1\) when \(A=Z\) and \(-1\) otherwise. For any policy with \(p=\Pr(A=1)\), \[J(p)=\tfrac12[(1-p)-p]+\tfrac12[p-(1-p)]=0.\] The verifier knows more than the agent, and can use the same backbone with that privileged context, but every admissible policy has the same value. The terminal reward may reveal the goal after the irreversible action; it cannot improve decisions on a fresh independent goal. Thus this argument does not assert zero mutual information with the full rewarded trajectory. Even an observable task with an already optimal initial policy prevents universal strict improvement.
checks.repair: State the structural mechanisms as possible sources of improvement, consistently with Lemma 2.1. Then \(\Delta J\ge\Delta_*-\varepsilon>0\). This uses the same evaluation return throughout and requires any training verifier to optimize that return or a proved calibrated surrogate. Establishing actionable feedback and such an optimization bound requires additional assumptions; privileged context alone supplies neither.

checks.repair:
Use \(\rho_\theta=\operatorname{Unif}(\Theta\cap B(\theta,r_N))\) whenever the intersection has positive Lebesgue volume. If \(V=\operatorname{vol}(\Theta)>0\), its exact penalty is
\[\operatorname{KL}(\rho_\theta\|\pi)=\log\frac{V}{\operatorname{vol}(\Theta\cap B(\theta,r_N))}.\]

checks.claim: The local odd cutoff functions have eigenvalues given by their Rayleigh quotients, whose inverse gives score fitting time P/sigma^nu for any isotropic kernel.
checks.explanation: A local Rayleigh quotient does not prove eigenfunction status or target spectral support, so it cannot imply a universal finite fitting time for isotropic kernels.
checks.demonstration: Take the positive-semidefinite isotropic kernel \(k(x,y)=(1+\cos(x-y))/2\), whose feature span is \(\{1,\cos x,\sin x\}\), and an equal Gaussian mixture centered at zero and \(\pi\). Both sine and cosine expectations vanish. Integration by parts gives \(\mathbb E[s]=0\), \(\mathbb E[s\cos X]=\mathbb E[\sin X]=0\), and \(\mathbb E[s\sin X]=-\mathbb E[\cos X]=0\) for its nonzero score \(s\). The score lies in the kernel nullspace, so zero-initialized kernel flow never learns it. Local quadratic kernel behavior and positive semidefiniteness hold.
checks.repair: Establish the approximate-eigenfunction and target spectral-support conditions needed for the fitting-time inference, or restrict it to kernels/settings for which those conditions are proved.
checks.scope: The universal spectral inference is unsupported. The local power counting and observed NTK/ReLU scaling are not refuted.

checks.demonstration: For centers zero and one, the product is \(x(x-1)e^{-(|x|+|x-1|)/\sigma}\). Under the equal two-Gaussian mixture, symmetry makes the two component integrals equal.
